```{r setup, include=FALSE}
knitr::opts_chunk$set(collapse = TRUE, comment = "#>", fig.width = 6, fig.height = 4)
library(gof)
```

These three procedures extend cumulative-residual model checking in different
directions. They answer different questions and retain distinct assumptions.
The examples use few simulations for speed; increase `R` for an analysis.

| Question | Endpoint | Null simulation |
|:--|:--|:--|
| Does a fitted mean model depart along any of several selected orderings? | `cumres_joint()` | Subject-coupled Gaussian multipliers and a maximum statistic. |
| Do Gaussian SEM residual distributions depart from normality? | `cumres_normality()` | Gaussian response simulation with a first-order nuisance-estimation correction. |
| How do residual diagnostics behave under a binomial/Poisson sampling model? | `cumres_bootstrap()` | Response simulation, with refitting for an estimated null. |

## Joint inference across orderings

The historical `cumres()` simulations provide marginal reference distributions.
Their saved columns are not joint draws across orderings. The new endpoint
keeps the same multiplier attached to a subject under every ordering.

```{r joint}
set.seed(1201)
d <- data.frame(x = seq(-2, 2, length.out = 160), z = rnorm(160))
d$y <- 1 + 0.6*d$x - 0.3*d$z + rnorm(nrow(d))
fit <- lm(y ~ x + z, data = d)

set.seed(1202)
joint <- fit |> cumres_joint(variable = c("x", "z"), R = 99, plots = 5)
joint |> as.data.frame()
plot(joint, idx = "x")
```

The table distinguishes `scope="marginal"` from `scope="family"`. The family
Sup statistic is the largest absolute process value over every chosen
ordering and evaluated point. The family `L2.range` statistic takes the
largest coordinate-range-normalized L2 norm. This normalization avoids
changing a family's relative coordinate weighting merely by changing units.
Individual `L2` rows retain the original unnormalized statistic.

The horizontal envelope is a simultaneous **null reference envelope**, not
a confidence interval for regression coefficients or fitted means. It applies
to the joint supported mean-model null, the chosen orderings and the evaluated
grid. It does not check every possible departure and does not supply strong
familywise error control for arbitrary separately interpreted component
hypotheses under partial alternatives.

Choose the ordering family, bandwidth and grid rule before inspecting the
responses. A finite grid cap limits the assertion to that grid. A numerically
indeterminate selected process withholds the family result instead of quietly
shrinking the family. Inspect `joint$joint` for the retained reference statistics,
adjusted marginal tails and envelope status.

## Gaussian SEM residual distributions

The existing SEM `cumres()` method checks mean/linearity. Normality requires a
different process: the empirical CDF of standardized marginal or projected
structural residuals, minus the standard Gaussian CDF. Fitted residuals cannot
be treated as if the parameters were known.

```{r normality}
set.seed(1203)
sem <- lava::lvm(y ~ x)
sem_data <- lava::sim(sem, 180)
sem_fit <- lava::estimate(sem, sem_data)

set.seed(1204)
normality <- sem_fit |> cumres_normality(R = 99, plots = 5)
normality |> as.data.frame()
plot(normality)
```

`variable=NULL` pools standardized marginal residual components. A single
named endogenous or latent variable selects its standardized projected
structural-error residual. Under the Gaussian SEM these linear residuals have
known standard normal marginal distributions at the true parameters.
The pooled component ECDF is not a universally consistent test of multivariate
normality or dependence.

The reference simulations implement the first-order correction in Sánchez,
Houseman and Ryan (2009), Section 3.1, equations (10)--(11). They use the joint
Gaussian likelihood score, expected information and the derivative of the
expected residual CDF. The correction includes parameters shared by the mean,
covariance and projection. This is an asymptotic fitted-model procedure, not
an ordinary known-parameter Kolmogorov--Smirnov test.

The horizontal coordinate is a fixed probability grid: at probability `u`,
the plotted process compares the residual ECDF at `qnorm(u)` with `u`.
Sup is the maximum on that grid; L2 integrates over probability using the
documented grid approximation. Finite grids approximate the full-domain
statistics in the paper.

Support is confined to complete, independent-subject Gaussian lava fits with
regular, identified nuisance information and valid structural moments.
Missing-data/FIML, clustered, weighted and boundary fits are outside this
endpoint. Observed exogenous covariates are held fixed. A projected residual
diagnostic may detect a distributional departure, but cannot uniquely attribute
it to one latent error when other model assumptions are false. A large p-value
does not establish that all latent or measurement errors are normal.

Finite-sample calibration needs care. In the qualification experiment with
200 cohorts of size 300 and `R=199`, inclusive `p <= 0.05` rejection rates
were 6--8.5% across the three residual modes and two statistics. The two
8.5% L2 results prompted a prespecified fresh paired study rather than being
dismissed because a broad screening check passed. With 200 fresh cohorts,
`R=399` and sample sizes 300/1,200, rates were 2.5--7% and 3.5--5%, respectively;
no fits were discarded or unresolved. All component-wise exact 95% binomial
intervals in the fresh study included 5%. This supports the bounded checks
without proving equivalence to 5% or a significant sample-size trend. Both
studies remain in the qualification record. The method is an asymptotic
diagnostic, not an exact finite-sample normality test.

## Binomial and Poisson parametric calibration

For a fitted canonical binomial/logit or Poisson/log model, this endpoint
simulates responses under the fitted distribution and refits each sample on
the same stored design, offsets and binomial trial counts. It does not run
an inner multiplier simulation or reevaluate the original user call.

```{r fitted-bootstrap}
set.seed(1205)
counts <- data.frame(x = seq(-1, 1, length.out = 100),
                     exposure = rep(c(1, 2), 50))
true_mean <- counts$exposure * exp(-1.5 + 0.5*counts$x)
counts$y <- rpois(nrow(counts), true_mean)
count_fit <- glm(y ~ x + offset(log(exposure)), data = counts, family = poisson())

set.seed(1206)
bootstrap <- count_fit |> cumres_bootstrap(variable = "x", R = 49, plots = 3)
bootstrap |> as.data.frame()
```

Ordering variables must be fixed design quantities. The fitted-prediction
ordering is rejected because freezing a response-dependent ordering would
define a different procedure. A single grid is selected and reused for the
observation and every simulated sample. Grouped binomial responses are
accumulated as success-minus-expected-success totals and normalized by the
square root of total trials, matching individual trial expansion at tied
ordering values. Nonunit positive Poisson prior weights are unsupported here:
their mean/variance interpretation alone does not specify a count sampler.

Fitted parametric bootstrap calibration remains approximate. It is a way to
use the assumed sampling distribution, not a guarantee that every sparse or
boundary-estimation problem has been solved.

A different mode tests a genuinely specified null:

```{r specified-null}
set.seed(1207)
specified <- count_fit |> cumres_bootstrap(
  variable = "x", R = 99, plots = 0,
  null = "specified", mean = true_mean
)
specified |> as.data.frame()
```

Here `true_mean` was specified before generating the observations. Under the
stated independent Poisson null, the observed and simulated statistics are
exchangeable conditional on the fixed design and grid. The plus-one rank
p-value controls finite-sample rejection probability, conservatively with
ties. Supplying means estimated from these observations does not have that
guarantee. The same distinction applies to specified binomial probabilities.

Every one of the `R` replicates is recorded. Some all-zero or all-successful
fits have analytically known boundary means and can be represented exactly.
Other separated, nonconverged or unresolved refits withhold the ordinary
p-value. `p.lower` and `p.upper` bound the tail calculation by assigning every
unresolved indicator zero or one; these are not confidence intervals.
Structurally certified zero-information processes keep zero statistics and
p-values of one even if another aspect of a replicate fit is unresolved.
Warnings, failure reasons and retained curve indices remain in
`bootstrap$bootstrap`. No successful-only resampling hides a fitting problem.
A fitted all-zero boundary null is degenerate and cannot assess unseen events.

## Reporting and reproducibility

All three endpoints accept the fitted model first and work with native `|>`.
`as.data.frame()`, `summary()` and optional tidiers retain their result labels
and method-specific metadata. Record the endpoint, its null interpretation,
selected family or residual projection, grid, bandwidth, `R`, seed and fitted
model/dependency versions with an analysis.

New endpoint Monte Carlo tails use `(1 + exceedances)/(R + 1)`. This avoids
reported zeros but does not make an asymptotic approximation exact. The
historical marginal `cumres()` convention is preserved for compatibility.
